title: Co-writing Tipitina with Professor Longhair
summary: Matassa helped organize the disorganized Tipitina session into a structure and clarified words, is a co-writer but does not take the money; the copyright has since been sold.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: In fact, did you know I'm a co-writer of Tipitina?
But how does that come about? Well, because it was disorganized. The session.
Tipitina was disorganized. It was a bunch of little one-line things between a bunch of piano playing.

And I helped organize it into a beginning, middle, and end, and like that. Contributed. Cleaned up. Clarified some of the words. You don't clarify much with Fess, but clarified some of the words. Mm-hmm. And gave it some structure. It was Fess's original thing. I didn't create it as such. But I helped make that record.
Mm-hmm. Do you have a credit on there? Do you have a? I used to be co-writer.
I don't take the money, though. It's supposed to be going to them.
Okay. I was just wondering. I thought you had a co-name with him.
But like I said, I was co-writer on it, but I don't take money for the song. And I presume it's going to them. It's supposed to.
Yeah. Well, I think he gets his royalties from it. The copyright's been sold. I think.
Yeah, right. Warner Chapel, I think, owns it now.
Yeah. Those packages have gone two or three steps now. Oh, yeah. One to the other. It's been sold somewhere. Yeah. The golden rule. He who has the gold makes the rules.
